 Oct 18, 2026 What Social Security’s 2027 COLA Update Means for Your Future Finances
 Written by Travis Woods | Edited by Angela Corry On Oct. 14, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. The COLA is what allows retirees to set their budgets for the new year and keep pace with changes in inflation, and the adjustment for 2027 is one of the most significant in decades.
 The 2027 COLA adjustment is the fifth highest in 35 years: 3.6%. That small financial bump each month will provide Social Security beneficiaries with more money to combat the pressure that cost of living puts on budgets.
 Read More: 3 Overlooked Social Security Rules That Could Add Thousands to Your Retirement Income   
 Find Out: 6 Clever Ways Retirees Are Earning Up to $1K Per Month From Home 
 How Much More Money Will You Get?
 The question most recipients are likely asking is “how much more money will I start receiving in January 2027?”
 Utilizing the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) August 2026 benefit figures, it is projected that the average Social Security beneficiary will receive approximately $75 more per month in 2027, and that average monthly benefits for workers with disabilities and survivor beneficiaries are expected to rise by about $59.
 Keep in mind, those figures are the average projections. The specific amount that you receive will depend on your current benefit level . For a quick calculus, a 3.6% adjustment adds roughly $36 for every $1,000 in monthly benefits that you receive (before any deductions).
 Impact of Medicare Premiums
 Most COLA changes are typically outpaced by the annual percentage increases in Part B premiums (for example, compare 2026’s COLA of 2.8% with the Part B hike of a staggering 9.7%). Often, Part B premiums can almost entirely obliterate the increase in Social Security benefits.
 However, as The Motley Fool notes, there’s a significant “silver lining” to the 2027 COLA.
 Per the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, though, the Part B premium increase for 2027 is only expected to be around 3.25% (or just $6.60, to a total of $209.50). If correct (the estimate has yet to be confirmed), that means 2027 would be the first year since 2023 in which a COLA (3.6%) would be larger than the Medicare Part B Premium hike (3.25%).
 For many, this is great news: If you are one of the tens of millions currently enrolled in traditional Medicare, you’ll actually be able to keep far more of next year’s COLA than in previous years, and put that money towards groceries and rent, or even set it aside for savings .
 Social Security’s Future
 The significant 2027 COLA arrives as Social Security is facing an existential crisis: the program’s reserves are expected to be depleted by the early 2030s, unless Congress intervenes.
 The program’s finances are tracked through two main trust funds: The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund pays retirement and survivor benefits, while the Disability Insurance (DI) Trust Fund pays disability benefits. The OASI faces the tighter timeline, as its reserves are projected to dry up by late 2032. Even then, Social Security won’t end, as ongoing payroll-tax revenue will still cover about 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits. Meanwhile, the DI fund is in stronger shape and is projected to last through 2100, per the SSA’s 2026 Trustees Report. 
 While the 3.6% COLA will indeed provide a small amount of monthly relief through 2027, the projected trust-fund shortfall for Social Security as a whole means that the program’s long-term future depends on congressional action, not a yearly adjustment. Until then, beneficiaries can use the COLA to help maintain purchasing power in an increasingly expensive economy.
